# 03.2 Nesting and Indentation: Organizing Your Code

## The Structure of an HTML Document

Imagine you're building a house. You wouldn't start nailing boards together without a blueprint, right? An HTML document is just like a digital house—it needs a clear, consistent structure so browsers (like Chrome or Firefox) know how to build the page correctly.

Every complete HTML page follows this skeleton:
- `<!DOCTYPE html>` — This tells the browser, "Hey, I'm an HTML5 document." Think of it as the seal on the blueprint.
- `<html>` — The root element that wraps everything else. This is the entire house frame.
  - `<head>` — The control room. It holds information *about* the page, like its title and settings.
  - `<body>` — The visible rooms. Everything you see on the page lives here.

Here's a minimal example:
```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My First Web Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <p>Hello, world!</p>
  </body>
</html>
```

Notice how elements are **nested**—each element is placed inside another. The `<title>` sits inside `<head>`, which sits inside `<html>`. This nesting is like stacking boxes: the smallest box goes inside a medium box, which goes inside the largest box.

Look at the sentence below. Identify the purpose of the `<head>` section in an HTML document. Write your answer in 1-3 sentences.

Sentence: The `<head>` element contains meta-information about the web page, such as its title and links to stylesheets.

```question eval="The student should mention that the <head> section contains meta-information about the web page, such as the title and links to stylesheets, and may explain that it is not displayed in the browser."
CORRECT: The <head> section contains metadata about the page, including the title and links to external resources like stylesheets.
CORRECT: It provides information about the document that is not displayed directly on the page, such as the title and CSS links.
INCORRECT: The <head> section contains the main content visible to users.
INCORRECT: It is used to display the page's body content.
```

## The Head: The Control Room

Let's zoom in on the `<head>` section. It doesn't display anything visible on the page, but it's crucial. The most common items inside `<head>` include:
- `<title>` — The text that appears in the browser tab.
- `<link>` — Used to connect stylesheets (we'll skip styles today).
- `<meta>` — Sets character encoding and other data.

Think of `<head>` as a room in the house labeled "Control Room." It has the light switches, the thermostat, and the security panel—stuff the residents (users) rarely see, but the house (browser) needs to run properly.

## The Body: Links and Images in Action

Now let's go into the visible space: the `<body>`. Here you put text, images, and links. Two of the most common elements are:
- **Anchor tag** (`<a>`): Creates a clickable link. It uses the `href` attribute to specify the destination.
  - Example: `<a href="https://example.com">Visit Example</a>`
- **Image tag** (`<img>`): Embeds an image. It uses `src` for the image URL and `alt` for a text description.
  - Example: `<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A beautiful sunset">`

The anchor tag can also open the link in a new tab by adding the `target="_blank"` attribute.

Formatted example in the body:
```html
<body>
  <h1>Welcome to My Site</h1>
  <p>Check out <a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">this cool link</a>!</p>
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/400/300" alt="Random image">
</body>
```

Write an HTML anchor tag that links to 'https://www.example.com' and opens the link in a new browser tab. Use proper attribute syntax.

```question eval="The student should provide an anchor tag <a> with href=\"https://www.example.com\" and target=\"_blank\" to open in a new tab. Including rel=\"noopener\" is optional but recommended."
CORRECT: <a href="https://www.example.com" target="_blank">Example</a>
CORRECT: <a target="_blank" href="https://www.example.com">Example</a>
INCORRECT: <a href="https://www.example.com">Example</a>
INCORRECT: <a href="www.example.com" target="_blank">Example</a>
```

## Nesting and Indentation: Keeping Your House Tidy

Look closely at the example above. Notice how each element is indented to show which element contains it. The `<h1>`, `<p>`, and `<img>` are all indented under `<body>`. Inside `<p>`, the `<a>` tag is indented further. This **indentation** is not required by the browser (your page will still work without it), but it's a **best practice** that makes code readable for humans.

**The nesting rule:** You must close the most recently opened tag before closing any outer tags.

Incorrect nesting:
```html
<p>This is <strong>bold text</p></strong>
<!-- Wrong: <strong> closes after <p> -->
```

Correct nesting:
```html
<p>This is <strong>bold text</strong></p>
<!-- Right: <strong> closes before <p> -->
```

Think of it like packing boxes for a move: you must close the small box before you close the larger box that contains it. If you try to close the big box first, the small box won't be secure.

Here's an example with poor nesting and no indentation:
```html
<body><h1>Title</h1><p>This is a <a href='https://example.com'>link</a> and an <img src='pic.jpg' alt='photo'></p></body>
```

And here it is with correct nesting and proper indentation (2 spaces per level):
```html
<body>
  <h1>Title</h1>
  <p>This is a <a href='https://example.com'>link</a> and an <img src='pic.jpg' alt='photo'></p>
</body>
```

## Your Turn: Practice Exercises

1. Write a complete HTML document (including `<!DOCTYPE html>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, `<title>`, and `<body>`) that displays a level-1 heading with the text "My Favorite Animal" and a paragraph with a link to a website about that animal.

2. Take the following incorrectly nested code and fix both the nesting and the indentation (use 2 spaces per level):
```html
<div><p>Visit our <a href='shop.html'>store</a></div></p>
```

## Summary and Review

- An HTML document always starts with `<!DOCTYPE html>` and has `<html>` wrapping `<head>` and `<body>`.
- `<head>` contains *invisible* information (like title), while `<body>` contains visible content.
- The anchor tag (`<a>`) uses the `href` attribute for the destination and `target="_blank"` to open in a new tab.
- The image tag (`<img>`) is self-closing and requires `src` and `alt` attributes.
- **Nesting** means putting one element inside another—you must close inner elements before outer ones.
- **Indentation** (2 spaces per level) makes code readable for you and other developers.
